scenes.visual: Title card 'Copy Yourself, or Be Copied' over a warm flask of pale yellow liquid. COLOUR MAP (both films): bacterial cell = pale GREEN rounded rod with a thin dark outline; bacterial chromosome = one BLUE loop; phage DNA = ORANGE strand; phage particle = cartoon with an ORANGE hexagon head, short grey tail and grey legs; food bar = GREEN, waste bar = BROWN. Counter box top right, white text on charcoal: 'cells: N' (film 2 adds a second box 'new phages: N'). All cells and phages are cartoons labelled 'schematic'; every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: One bacterium and one virus land in a warm flask full of food. An hour later, which has made more of itself? And how did it do it?
scenes.visual: Camera drops into the flask: one GREEN rod-shaped bacterium and one ORANGE-headed phage drift in side by side. A stopwatch labelled '1 hour' ticks in the corner. Question card fades in: 'which makes more of itself, and how?'
scenes.narration: One bacterium and one virus land in a warm flask full of food. An hour later, which has made more of itself? And how did it do it?

scenes.tts: Start with the bacterium. It is a single cell, with its D N A in one loop called the chromosome. There is no nucleus around it.
scenes.caption: Start with the bacterium. It is a single cell, with its DNA in one loop called the chromosome. There is no nucleus around it.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the rod. A BLUE loop slowly rotates inside it; label 'chromosome (the cell's main DNA)'. A dashed circle where a nucleus would be appears, then is crossed out: 'no nucleus'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Start with the bacterium. It is a single cell, with its DNA in one loop called the chromosome. There is no nucleus around it.

scenes.tts: First the cell copies its chromosome. Then it grows longer, with one copy at each end. Then it pinches in the middle and splits in two.
scenes.visual: The BLUE loop duplicates into two BLUE loops; the rod stretches, the two loops slide to opposite ends; a waist forms in the middle and closes. Step labels appear in turn: '1 copy', '2 grow', '3 split'. Counter top right ticks 'cells: 1' to 'cells: 2'.
scenes.narration: First the cell copies its chromosome. Then it grows longer, with one copy at each end. Then it pinches in the middle and splits in two.

scenes.tts: This is binary fission. Each new cell gets a complete copy of the chromosome. So the two cells match, except for rare copying mistakes.
scenes.visual: Banner 'binary fission'. The two daughter rods sit side by side, each with one whole BLUE loop; an '=' sign between them. A tiny red dot flickers on one loop with the label 'rare copying mistake'.
scenes.narration: This is binary fission. Each new cell gets a complete copy of the chromosome. So the two cells match, except for rare copying mistakes.

scenes.tts: Now each new cell does the same thing. One becomes two. Two become four, then eight, then sixteen. Every round doubles the count.
scenes.visual: Both rods split together, then all four, then all eight; the screen fills with GREEN rods, each with a BLUE loop. Counter steps 'cells: 2', '4', '8', '16' in time with each split. A small label under the counter: 'one doubling per round'.
scenes.narration: Now each new cell does the same thing. One becomes two. Two become four, then eight, then sixteen. Every round doubles the count.

scenes.tts: The time for one round is called the doubling time. In the best lab conditions, an E coli cell can double about every twenty minutes.
scenes.caption: The time for one round is called the doubling time. In the best lab conditions, an E. coli cell can double about every 20 minutes.
scenes.visual: A clock face appears beside the counter; its hand sweeps one third of the way round as one rod splits. Label 'doubling time'. Text card: 'E. coli, best lab conditions: about 20 min'.
scenes.narration: The time for one round is called the doubling time. In the best lab conditions, an E. coli cell can double about every 20 minutes.

scenes.tts: Keep that pace for seven hours, with no cells dying. Will one cell become closer to a thousand cells, or closer to a million?
scenes.visual: Counter resets to 'cells: 1'. Card: '20 min per doubling, 7 hours'. Two choice boxes: 'about 1,000?' and 'about 1,000,000?'.
scenes.narration: Keep that pace for seven hours, with no cells dying. Will one cell become closer to a thousand cells, or closer to a million?

scenes.visual: The two choice boxes pulse gently; the clock waits at 0.

scenes.tts: More than a million. The counter reaches twenty-one doublings, about two million cells. That is a calculated number, not a count of real cells.
scenes.caption: More than a million. The counter reaches 21 doublings, about two million cells. That is a calculated number, not a count of real cells.
scenes.visual: The clock spins through 7 hours; the counter races up to '21 doublings' and 'cells: 2,097,152'. The 'about 1,000,000?' box lights. Stamp under the counter: 'calculated, not counted'. Rods shrink to a dense green haze.
scenes.narration: More than a million. The counter reaches 21 doublings, about two million cells. That is a calculated number, not a count of real cells.

scenes.tts: But a real flask is closed. As the cells multiply, they use up the food. Their wastes build up in the liquid around them.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole flask, now cloudy. Beside it, a GREEN food bar drains from full toward empty while a BROWN waste bar rises. The counter keeps climbing, more slowly.
scenes.narration: But a real flask is closed. As the cells multiply, they use up the food. Their wastes build up in the liquid around them.

scenes.tts: So the climb slows, and the count levels off. Doubling makes numbers huge, but only while food lasts and wastes stay low.
scenes.visual: A small curve draws itself under the flask: flat, steep rise, then flat top, labelled 'schematic'. The counter freezes as the curve flattens. Labels on the flat top: 'food low', 'wastes high'.
scenes.narration: So the climb slows, and the count levels off. Doubling makes numbers huge, but only while food lasts and wastes stay low.

scenes.tts: Now the virus. This one is a phage, a virus that infects bacteria. Left alone in all that food, what does it do?
scenes.visual: Cut to the lone ORANGE-headed phage floating in clear liquid, away from any cells. Label 'phage (bacteriophage)'. Its own counter box shows 'phages: 1'. Food particles drift past it.
scenes.narration: Now the virus. This one is a phage, a virus that infects bacteria. Left alone in all that food, what does it do?

scenes.tts: Nothing. It does not grow. It does not split. It cannot make anything on its own. Its counter stays at one.
scenes.visual: Food particles bounce off the phage. Three labels appear and are each crossed out: 'grow', 'split', 'make anything'. The counter 'phages: 1' stays fixed while a clock beside it spins.
scenes.narration: Nothing. It does not grow. It does not split. It cannot make anything on its own. Its counter stays at one.

scenes.tts: Then it lands on a bacterium and injects its D N A. Soon, orange phage parts start to appear inside the cell.
scenes.caption: Then it lands on a bacterium and injects its DNA. Soon, orange phage parts start to appear inside the cell.
scenes.visual: The phage drifts onto a GREEN rod and attaches by its legs; an ORANGE strand slides from its head into the cell. Inside, small ORANGE hexagon heads and grey tail pieces appear one by one, separate, not joined. Label 'phage parts'.
scenes.narration: Then it lands on a bacterium and injects its DNA. Soon, orange phage parts start to appear inside the cell.

scenes.tts: The phage is not making them. The cell is. The cell reads the phage genes as if they were its own, and builds phage parts.
scenes.visual: Spotlight on the cell's own machinery, drawn as small grey workbench blocks labelled 'host machinery'. The ORANGE strand feeds into a block like a recipe card, and ORANGE parts come out. The empty phage coat outside is dimmed, label 'doing nothing'.
scenes.narration: The phage is not making them. The cell is. The cell reads the phage genes as if they were its own, and builds phage parts.

scenes.tts: So the two multiply in opposite ways. The bacterium grows and splits on its own. The virus never divides. A host cell builds every new virus.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: GREEN rods splitting, counter 'cells' climbing, label 'copies itself'. Right: one cell full of ORANGE parts, label 'is copied, by a host cell'. Middle divider labelled 'two ways to multiply'.
scenes.narration: So the two multiply in opposite ways. The bacterium grows and splits on its own. The virus never divides. A host cell builds every new virus.

scenes.tts: Here is the one rule to keep from this film. A bacterium copies itself. A virus is copied by a host cell, never by itself.
scenes.visual: The split screen holds; the two labels 'copies itself' and 'is copied, by a host cell' grow larger and settle under each half.
scenes.narration: Here is the one rule to keep from this film. A bacterium copies itself. A virus is copied by a host cell, never by itself.

scenes.visual: Hex end card with one line only: 'A bacterium copies itself; a virus is copied by a host cell.'
